sm: Georgia Howe opens the Monday, November 23rd edition, filling in while John is out. The top story is that Democrats are threatening a government shutdown in response to escalating strikes in the Middle East, with a congressman calling the zeroing out of funding for Iran combat operations a huge red line. The show also previews two other stories. A key FBI criminal database has been hacked, raising the question of whether crucial information is now compromised. And Mexican officials have captured a cartel boss who was on the FBI's most wanted list.

Daily Wire contributor Tim Pierce recaps a weekend of fresh aggression from Iran. The Houthis, an Iranian proxy group, claimed two strikes on Saudi Arabia, one on a coastal oil refinery and one on a radar near Riyadh, though a single drone headed for Riyadh was reportedly shot down. The Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps launched a drone and ballistic missile attack on Bahrain, which Bahrain said wounded two people and set a civilian industrial facility on fire. The IRGC said it was targeting the US military, since the Fifth Fleet is based there. Iran has tried several times in the past week to hit US sites in Bahrain while saying it is open to a negotiated end to the war. Pierce says the Wall Street Journal links Iran's harder line to the Democratic midterm victory, since Democrats who campaigned against military action in Iran will soon control Congress. Congressman Ro Khanna is heard saying zeroing out Iran combat funding is a red line, even if it means a government shutdown. Pierce adds that the strikes may also test how Bahrain and Saudi Arabia respond to Iranian pressure. President Trump, on Fox News, says he will not budge on Iran ever having a nuclear weapon and wants a permanent deal. CBS News reports that US and Israeli officials are weighing more joint strikes, as Netanyahu worries about how fast Iran is rebuilding its ballistic missile stockpile, and Trump has said Iran may be pursuing chemical and biological weapons.

A retired FBI agent describes the National Crime Information Center as the lifeblood of state and local law enforcement, used to check warrants, criminal histories and missing persons during stops. Former federal prosecutor Zach Smith of the Heritage Foundation says much is still unknown about the weekend hack, including what was accessed and what the hackers might gain. He notes the database is used by most agencies and by prosecutors in nearly every case. Altering records is typically harder, but the FBI will be checking logs for changes, which would be most dangerous for officers deciding whether to approach someone with backup. He thinks it more likely that hackers harvested information to sell or misuse. The database holds many personal details but no classified material or the most sensitive investigative files. Smith says Americans are right to be concerned after recent outages and leaks, though caution is needed. This follows another reported breach of the FBI's jobs portal and personnel information, and large law enforcement agencies are target-rich for hackers. His advice is that the FBI's top priority should be determining how the breach happened and confirming nothing was altered.

Daily Wire reporter Jacob Wheeler explains that Mexican forces arrested a cartel boss who was on the FBI's top ten most wanted list. The 44-year-old led a faction of a cartel in northwestern Mexico and moved cocaine, methamphetamine, heroin and marijuana into the United States. He was first indicted in 2012, a superseding indictment and federal warrant followed in 2019, and the Justice Department offered a five million dollar reward. Homeland Security Investigations called the arrest a coordinated effort, and it appears the two governments shared intelligence for weeks, with American intelligence leading Mexican special forces to him in a bloody Friday night raid. This comes amid President Trump's crackdown on cartels, including his blunt talk with Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum at a summit in China and an executive order designating cartels as terrorist organizations. Wheeler says removing a boss does not remove a cartel and usually creates a violent power struggle. At least four Mexican soldiers and seven gunmen were killed. The Wall Street Journal expects his second in command, known as the Musician, to take over, but warns succession may be complicated and violent. Georgia Howe calls it whack-a-mole.
